messages.content: Maintain a 2:1 ratio of declarative to interrogative sentences in your response. Show a metric space (M, d) is complete if and only if any sequence (F_n) of nonempty closed subsets of M with - F_{n+1} \subset F_n - diam F_n \rightarrow 0 as n \rightarrow \infty has a nonempty intersection

message.content:
A metric space is complete exactly when every Cauchy sequence converges in M.
Why should completeness force a common point?
If M is complete, choose x_n in F_n for the given nonempty nested F_n and use d(x_n,x_{n+1}) \le diam F_n to get a Cauchy sequence converging to x.
Since each F_n is closed and contains all later terms, x belongs to every F_n.
Conversely, how can the diameter condition detect completeness?
Given a Cauchy sequence y_n, define G_n = closure of {y_k : k >= n}.
The sets G_n are nonempty closed nested sets, and diam G_n \rightarrow 0.
What does the hypothesis give now?
It gives a point z in the intersection of all G_n.
Since each G_n contains a tail of the sequence (y_n), z is the limit of that sequence.
Does that complete the equivalence?
Therefore every Cauchy sequence converges, so the nested-diameter intersection property is equivalent to completeness.
